title: Everyday Hebrew
hook: todah, b'ezrat Hashem, mazal tov, l'chaim

segments.voice: Yesterday, gematria: letters read as numbers, chai as eighteen, and Abram's three hundred and eighteen as one man, Eliezer. Your line was letters count. Did a number make you look twice? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-four.

A grandmother hangs up the phone in her kitchen. Good news: the baby has arrived, a girl, and everyone is well. Within a minute the room has said four things. Mazal tov, from everyone at once. B'ezrat Hashem, from the grandmother, when someone asks when they'll get to visit. Someone finds a bottle, pours, lifts a glass: l'chaim. And when the glass is handed across the table, a quiet todah. None of it is a prayer service. It's just a kitchen. But Hebrew is doing a lot of work in that room. Today, four phrases that turn up in ordinary Jewish life, and the smallest of them, which carries a whole root inside it.
screen: `A PHONE CALL: A BABY GIRL.` → `FOUR PHRASES IN A MINUTE.` → `THE SMALLEST ONE.`

segments.voice: Everyday Hebrew. Take the phrases one at a time. First, mazal tov. People say it at a birth, a wedding, a new job, a finished exam. It works like congratulations; mazal is usually translated luck or fortune, and tov is good. Second, b'ezrat Hashem: with the help of the Name. You met Hashem two days ago. Some Jews tuck this phrase into talk about the future, when they'll visit, when the house will be finished, a small way of saying the plans aren't only theirs. Third, l'chaim, to life: the same chai you added up yesterday, eighteen. Fourth, todah. Thank you. It's the plainest of the four, and its root runs back into Genesis. It comes from the letters yod, dalet, heh, which carry thanks and acknowledgment. In Genesis, when Leah gives birth to yet another son, she says, "Now will I praise the LORD: therefore she called his name Judah." In Hebrew, Yehudah, from the same root as todah. The psalm that repeats its refrain verse after verse opens with the same root: "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good." In Hebrew, hodu. And the short prayer some Jews say on waking, before anything else, begins modeh ani: I give thanks. Same root again. So the word for passing the salt shares its root with the name Leah gave a son, and with the first word of a morning prayer. Todah.
screen: `MAZAL TOV: GOOD FORTUNE.` · `B'EZRAT HASHEM: WITH GOD'S HELP.` · `L'CHAIM: TO LIFE.` · `TODAH: THE ROOT OF THANKS.` · then, large: `TODAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say todah. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one person who did something for you this week that you never properly thanked. Something small is fine: a ride, a text, a door held. See their face. Say the word silently, toward them: todah. Then a second person. Then something that isn't a person at all: the bed you slept in, the water in the tap, the breath you're taking now. Todah for each. If you pray, you can say modeh ani, I give thanks, the way some Jews begin each morning. The bell holds the time.

segments.voice: Everyday Hebrew. Mazal tov, b'ezrat Hashem, l'chaim, and todah, thank you, from the root of Judah's name. Today's word.
Your line: todah. Today, say it out loud once, to a real person, in Hebrew or in English, for something you'd usually let pass. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-four.
